excerpt: Georgia's Super Speeder Law adds a $200 surcharge for driving 75+ mph on a two-lane road or 85+ mph anywhere, with license suspension if unpaid within 120 days.
keyTakeaways: Georgia's Super Speeder Law (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b)) imposes an additional $200 surcharge on drivers convicted of 75+ mph on two-lane roads or 85+ mph anywhere, with automatic license suspension for non-payment within 120 days. South Carolina has no equivalent law; it fines speeding on a tiered scale that tops out at $75-$200 or 30 days in jail for 25+ mph over (S.C. Code § 56-5-1520), and can charge reckless driving (S.C. Code § 56-5-2920) where the speed shows wilful or wanton disregard for safety. Proof that a driver was speeding establishes negligence per se (duty and breach) in both states; the injured person must still prove causation and damages, and modified comparative fault then applies (Georgia bars recovery at 50% fault, South Carolina at 51%).

faqs.question: What is a Super Speeder in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Under Georgia's Super Speeder Law (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b)), a driver convicted of traveling 75 mph or faster on a two-lane road or 85 mph or faster on any road is classified as a Super Speeder and must pay an additional $200 state surcharge on top of the original speeding fine and court costs.

faqs.question: What happens if I do not pay the Super Speeder fee?
faqs.answer: If you fail to pay the $200 Super Speeder fee within 120 days of the Georgia DDS notice, your driver's license is automatically suspended. Reinstatement requires paying the original $200 fee plus a $50 reinstatement fee. Driving on a suspended license is a misdemeanor under O.C.G.A. § 40-5-121.

faqs.question: Does South Carolina have a Super Speeder law?
faqs.answer: No. South Carolina does not have a Super Speeder equivalent. Speeding is fined on a tiered scale, and 25 mph or more over the limit carries $75 to $200 or up to 30 days in jail for a first offense plus six license points (S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1520, 56-1-720). Excessive speed can also be charged as reckless driving under S.C. Code § 56-5-2920 — $25 to $200 or up to 30 days — but the statute sets no speed threshold.

faqs.question: Can an out-of-state driver get a Super Speeder designation?
faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia's Super Speeder Law applies equally to out-of-state drivers. If you fail to pay the $200 fee, Georgia suspends your privilege to drive in the state and notifies your home state through the Driver License Compact, which may result in your home state taking additional action against your license.

faqs.question: How does a Super Speeder conviction affect a personal injury claim?
faqs.answer: Proof that the driver was speeding can establish negligence per se, meaning the violation supplies the duty and breach elements of negligence; the injured person still has to prove the speed caused the crash and the injuries. The ticket and the conviction themselves, including a Super Speeder conviction, are generally not admissible in a civil case in Georgia or South Carolina (Howard v. Lay, 259 Ga. App. 391 (2003); S.C. Code § 56-5-6160), but a guilty plea to the ticket can be used as an admission.

faqs.question: Can I get punitive damages if a speeding driver caused my accident?
faqs.answer: Potentially yes. If the speeding driver's conduct rises to willful misconduct or conscious indifference to consequences, punitive damages may be available. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases, with no cap where the driver intended to cause harm or was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(f)-(g)). South Carolina caps them at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 — a floor indexed to inflation and set at $739,245 for 2026 — and removes the cap where the driver was substantially impaired (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).
